title: Staying Present for Your Kid(s) After Loss
subtitle: Parenting through grief while helping your children grieve
summary: **Your children lost a parent.** You lost your spouse. And somehow, while drowning in your own grief, you are expected to help them navigate theirs. This is one of the hardest aspects of widowed parenting. This journey helps you understand what your children are experiencing, gives you permission to grieve while parenting, and offers practical guidance for being present for your kids without losing yourself in the process. Grounded in Scripture and informed by how children process loss, this journey walks with you through the impossible task of parenting through grief.

cover.heroImageDescription: A parent and child together, perhaps looking at a photo or walking hand in hand, representing the journey of grieving together while still connected.

targetOutcomes: Understand how children grieve differently at different ages
Learn to balance your own grief with your children's needs
Develop ways to talk about your spouse with your children
Create space for your children to express their grief
Build new family rhythms while honoring the past
Find support for your dual role as grieving spouse and grieving parent

activities.title: The Impossible Task: Parenting While Grieving
activities.subtitle: Acknowledging the weight of what you are carrying
activities.whyThisMatters: Before you can navigate parenting through grief, you need to acknowledge how impossibly hard this is and give yourself permission to be imperfect at it.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Healing begins with acknowledging the reality of what you are facing.

cards.title: You Are Being Asked to Do the Impossible
cards.text:
**Let us name what is happening here.**

**Your world has collapsed.** The person you built your life with is gone. You are drowning in grief, barely able to function some days, unsure how you will survive the next hour let alone the next year.

**And you have children who need you.**

**They need you to be present when you can barely be present to yourself.** They need you to help them grieve when you do not know how to handle your own grief. They need stability when everything in your life has become unstable.

**This is an impossible task.** Read that again: impossible. Not difficult. Not challenging. Impossible, in the sense that no human being can do this perfectly.

**You will fail at it.** Not because you are weak or bad at parenting, but because you are being asked to do something that cannot be done well in your own strength. There is not enough of you.

**But here is the hope Scripture offers: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9|My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness).** God does not expect you to have enough. He offers to be enough when you are not.

**Acknowledging this is not giving up.** It is giving yourself permission to be imperfect. To do the best you can with what you have. To accept help, both human and divine. To forgive yourself when you fall short.

**You are doing the impossible.** Grace is required. And grace is available.

cards.title: They Lost a Parent. You Lost Your Person.
cards.text:
**Your children's loss is real and devastating.** But it is a different loss than yours.

**They lost a parent.** Someone who was supposed to be there for their whole childhood. Someone who would have walked them through milestones. Someone whose absence creates a hole in their development.

**You lost your spouse.** Your partner. The person who shared your bed, your dreams, your daily life. The person who was supposed to grow old with you. The person who was parenting alongside you.

**Scripture speaks to both losses.** For children who lose parents, James 1:27|a husband to the widow calls the fatherless the special concern of God. For spouses who lose partners, God describes Himself as "a husband to the widow" (Isaiah 54:5|a husband to the widow). Both losses matter to Him.

**Both losses are profound.** But they are not the same.

**You cannot fully understand what your children are experiencing, and they cannot fully understand what you are experiencing.** You are grieving together, but you are grieving different things.

**This can create isolation even within your own family.** Each person in their own bubble of pain, unable to fully reach each other.

**But it can also create connection.** You are the only people who lost this specific person. You share something no one else shares. You can grieve together even when you are grieving differently.

**God sees each of your griefs distinctly.** He is close to you in your widowhood. He is close to your children in their loss of a parent. He holds all of you.

cards.title: The Pressure to Be Strong
cards.text:
**People will tell you to be strong for your children.** They mean well. They are wrong.

**The idea that you must hide your grief to protect your children teaches them that grief is shameful.** That sadness should be hidden. That the appropriate response to devastating loss is to pretend everything is fine.

**Your children do not need you to be strong.** They need you to be real.

**Scripture is filled with people who grieved openly.** David wept over Absalom so loudly the whole army heard (2 (Samuel 19:1-4). Jacob mourned Joseph with such intensity that his family became concerned (Genesis 37:34-35). Jesus wept publicly at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35). None of these were failures of strength. They were honest expressions of love in the face of loss.

**Your children need to see that it is okay to cry.** That grief is a normal response to loss. That even adults struggle when someone they love dies.

**This does not mean you fall apart in front of them constantly or make them responsible for your emotional wellbeing.** There is a balance between hiding your grief completely and overwhelming them with it.

**But the pressure to be strong, to hold it together, to never let them see you struggle, that pressure will break you.** And it will teach your children to suppress their own grief.

**You can be honest with your children about how hard this is while still being a safe presence for them.** Those are not mutually exclusive. Jesus was both.

cards.title: Your Current State
cards.text: How are you balancing your own grief with parenting right now? Where is it working, and where is it breaking down?

cards.title: What You Need to Hear
cards.text:
**Take a moment to give yourself some truths you need to hear, grounded in what Scripture says about you.**

**You are doing the best you can in an impossible situation.** God sees your effort and calls it faithful, not inadequate.

**Your children do not need a perfect parent.** They need a present one, even if that presence is imperfect. "A bruised reed he will not break" (Isaiah 42:3|A bruised reed he will not break). You are bruised, not broken.

**Your grief matters.** You do not have to abandon it to care for your children. "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted" (Matthew 5:4|A bruised reed he will not break). That blessing is for you too, not just your children.

**Asking for help is not failure.** It is wisdom. Moses needed Aaron and Hur to hold up his arms (Exodus 17:12|Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted). You need people to hold up yours.

**Getting this wrong sometimes does not make you a bad parent.** It makes you a grieving human doing something impossibly hard. God's mercies are new every morning (Lamentations 3:23).

**Write what you need to hear.** Return to it when the guilt or pressure becomes too much.
cards.reflection: What truths do you need to hear about parenting through grief?

cards.title: Permission to Be Imperfect
cards.text:
**Give yourself explicit permission to be imperfect at this.**

**I give myself permission to grieve while parenting, knowing that both are sacred tasks.**

**I give myself permission to not have all the answers for my children.** Only God knows all things.

**I give myself permission to let them see that I am struggling.** Honesty is not weakness.

**I give myself permission to ask for help when I need it.** This is wisdom, not failure.

**I give myself permission to fail sometimes and try again.** His mercies are new every morning.

**I give myself permission to take care of myself so I can take care of them.** I cannot pour from an empty cup.

**I am doing the impossible.** I will do it imperfectly. God's grace is sufficient.

**Write this permission in your own words.** You will need to return to it.
cards.reflection: **Write your permission to be imperfect.**

activities.title: How Children Grieve: Understanding Their Experience
activities.subtitle: Recognizing grief at different ages and stages
activities.whyThisMatters: Children grieve differently than adults and differently at different ages. Understanding this helps you recognize and support their grief.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Children's grief expressions are shaped by their developmental stage and cognitive capacity.

cards.title: Grief Looks Different in Children
cards.text:
**When Sarah's husband died, her seven-year-old seemed fine.** He went to school, played with friends, laughed at cartoons. She wondered if something was wrong with him. Did he not understand? Did he not care?

**Then one night, three weeks later, he crawled into her bed sobbing and asked if she was going to die too.**

**Children do not grieve like adults.** They cannot sustain the emotional weight the way we can. Instead, they grieve in bursts. They step into grief, feel it intensely, and then step out again to play, to be normal, to be children.

**This is not denial or lack of feeling.** It is how children protect themselves from being overwhelmed. They can only hold grief for so long before they need relief.

**Your child may seem fine and then fall apart without warning.** They may ask devastating questions at random moments. They may seem to have forgotten and then suddenly remember with full force.

**This is normal.** It is how children grieve. It is not a sign that something is wrong. Jesus said, "Let the little children come to me" (Matthew 19:14|Let the little children come to me). He receives them as they are, including how they grieve. So can you.

cards.title: Young Children: Ages 3-5
cards.text:
**Young children do not understand death as permanent.** They may ask when the parent is coming back, over and over, not because they have forgotten but because their minds cannot grasp forever.

**They think magically.** They may believe they caused the death somehow, by being bad or wishing something. They need repeated reassurance that it was not their fault.

**They express grief through behavior more than words.** Regression to younger behaviors, bedwetting, clinginess, tantrums. These are grief expressed the only way they know how.

**They need concrete, simple explanations.** Their parent's body stopped working and could not be fixed. Avoid euphemisms like "sleeping" or "passed away" that confuse more than help.

**They need routine.** Predictability is security. Keep as much of their normal life intact as possible. "Train up a child in the way he should go" (Proverbs 22:6|sleeping) includes providing the stability they need to feel safe.

**They need physical comfort.** Hugs, presence, reassurance that you are still here. Their deepest fear is losing you too. Remind them often: I am here. I am not going anywhere. God is watching over all of us.

cards.title: School-Age Children: Ages 6-12
cards.text:
**School-age children understand that death is permanent.** This knowledge makes them more anxious, not less. They know their parent is not coming back. They know you could die too.

**They ask questions, sometimes uncomfortable ones.** How did they die? What happens to the body? Will it happen to me? Answer honestly at their level. They can handle truth better than uncertainty.

**This is an age where faith can become deeply meaningful.** Children this age can understand that their parent is with God. They can find comfort in Jesus's words: "In my Father's house are many rooms... I am going there to prepare a place for you" (John 14:2|In my Father's house are many rooms... I am going there to prepare a place for you). Heaven becomes real to them.

**They may worry about practical things.** Who will pick me up from school? Who will coach my team? They are trying to understand how life works now.

**They may try to take care of you.** Children this age can become parentified, sensing your grief and trying to manage it. They need permission to be children, not your caretakers.

**They are watching how you grieve.** They are learning from you how to handle loss. This is both pressure and opportunity. Let them see you bring grief to God. Let them see faith in action during hardship.

cards.title: Teenagers: Ages 13-18
cards.text:
**Teenagers grieve in complex ways that can be hard to read.**

**They may pull away, retreating into their rooms, their phones, their friend groups.** This can look like not caring when it is actually self-protection.

**They may act out.** Risk-taking behavior, anger, defiance. Grief in teenagers often looks like rebellion. Do not dismiss behavior problems without considering that grief may be underneath.

**They may seem fine, compartmentalizing grief to function at school and with friends.** This is not denial. It is coping.

**They understand death fully, including its implications.** They grieve the future their parent will not see. Graduation. Marriage. Grandchildren. Help them imagine that their parent will be watching from heaven, that the separation is temporary.

**They may resist talking to you.** A counselor, another trusted adult, or a grief group for teens might reach them better. This is not rejection of you. It is developmental normalcy.

**They need you to be present without being intrusive.** Available but not hovering. Checking in without interrogating. "Be quick to listen, slow to speak" (James 1:19|Be quick to listen, slow to speak) is particularly important with grieving teenagers.

**And they need permission to still be teenagers.** To have fun. To not be defined by their grief. To live their lives even though their parent died.

cards.title: Your Children's Grief
cards.text:
**Think about each of your children and how they are experiencing grief.**

What age and stage are they at?

How have you seen their grief expressed? What behaviors or words have shown their grief?

What questions have they asked, or what questions do you sense they are holding?

What do they seem to need that they may not be getting?

What is working in how you are supporting their grief?

How can you point them toward God's comfort in age-appropriate ways?

**Understanding where your children are helps you meet them there rather than expecting them to grieve the way you do.**
cards.reflection: How is each of your children experiencing and expressing grief?

cards.title: One Thing for Each Child
cards.text:
**Based on what you know about how your children are grieving, identify one thing you can do for each child this week.**

**It might be having a conversation about their parent.**

**It might be creating space for them to ask questions.**

**It might be letting them know it is okay to be sad, or okay to be happy.**

**It might be watching for behavioral signals you have been missing.**

**It might be connecting them with additional support.**

**It might be reading a Scripture about heaven together.**

**It might be simply saying, "I miss them too.**"

**Choose one thing for each child.** Not everything. Just one thing that meets them where they are.

**"Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4|I miss them too.**).** That instruction includes teaching them to grieve with hope.
cards.reflection: What is one thing you can do for each of your children this week to support their grief?

activities.title: Talking About Them: Keeping Your Spouse Present for Your Children
activities.subtitle: How to speak about your spouse in ways that help your children
activities.whyThisMatters: Your children need to know their parent, remember their parent, and have permission to talk about their parent. You are the keeper of those stories now.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Maintaining connection to deceased loved ones through memory and conversation supports healthy grief.

cards.title: You Are the Keeper of Stories
cards.text:
**Your spouse is gone.** But their story does not have to be.

**You hold memories your children do not have.** Stories from before they were born. Details about who their parent was as a person, not just as a parent. The history that made your spouse who they were.

**You are the keeper of these stories now.** The one who can tell your children about their parent's childhood, their dreams, their quirks, their journey.

**Scripture places great value on remembering and passing down stories.** "Tell it to your children, and let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation" (Joel 1:3|Tell it to your children, and let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation). God commanded Israel to tell the next generation what He had done. You have a similar calling: to tell your children who their parent was.

**Telling these stories may be painful.** You may cry. That is okay. Tears do not hurt your children as much as silence does.

**Your spouse deserves to be remembered.** Your children deserve to know them. You are the bridge between the two.

cards.title: Creating Space for Conversation
cards.text:
**Children often want to talk about their deceased parent but do not know if it is allowed.** They watch your cues. If you never bring up their parent, they may think the topic is forbidden.

**Create space by mentioning your spouse naturally.** "Your dad loved this song." "Your mom would have laughed at that." "Remember when we all went to the beach?"

**These casual mentions give permission.** They say: we can talk about them here. Their name is not forbidden.

**Ask questions too.** "Do you remember when your dad taught you to ride a bike?" "What do you miss about your mom?" "Is there anything you wish you could ask them?"

**Some conversations will happen at inconvenient times.** In the car, at bedtime, in the middle of dinner. Children bring things up when they feel ready, not when it is scheduled. Be available for those moments.

**You do not have to have all the answers.** Sometimes the best response is "I miss them too. Let us talk about them."

**The book of Deuteronomy instructs parents: "Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up" (Deuteronomy 6:7|I miss them too. Let us talk about them.).** Talk about your spouse the same way: woven into ordinary life.

cards.title: Honest but Age-Appropriate
cards.text:
**When Michael's children asked about their mother's death, he did not know what to say.** She had died of cancer, but the details were brutal. How much should they know?

**He found a middle path: honest but age-appropriate.** "She was very sick, and the doctors tried everything, but her body could not fight anymore. It was not her fault, and it was not anyone's fault. She did not want to leave you. And she is with Jesus now, and she is not in pain anymore."

**The children asked more questions over time.** He answered each one honestly, giving them as much truth as they could handle at their age.

**Your children need honesty.** Lies or evasions will eventually be discovered and will damage trust. But they do not need every detail.

**Match your honesty to their developmental level.** A five-year-old needs simple truth. A fifteen-year-old can handle more complexity.

**And when you do not know the answer, say so.** "I do not know why this happened. I wish I did." It is okay to not have explanations for the unexplainable. Even Jesus's closest followers did not always understand God's plans.

**But always, always point them to hope: "We believe that Jesus died and rose again, and so we believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in him" (1 Thessalonians 4:14|We believe that Jesus died and rose again, and so we believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in him).**

cards.title: Talking About Your Spouse
cards.text: How comfortable are you talking about your spouse with your children? What makes it easy or hard?

cards.title: Stories to Tell
cards.text:
**Think about stories and information your children should know about their parent.**

What stories from your spouse's childhood or young adulthood would help your children know them better?

What did your spouse love? Hobbies, passions, interests?

What were they like as a person? Their personality, their quirks, what made them unique?

What did they dream of? Hopes they had for themselves, for your family, for your children?

What was their faith like? How did they relate to God?

What did they love about each of your children specifically?

**These stories are treasures.** Start gathering them, writing them down if needed, so they are not lost. "A good person leaves an inheritance for their children's children" (Proverbs 13:22|A good person leaves an inheritance for their children's children). These stories are part of your spouse's inheritance to your children.
cards.reflection: What stories and information about your spouse should your children know?

cards.title: Start a Conversation
cards.text:
**This week, intentionally start a conversation with your children about their parent.**

**It could be looking at photos together.** "I love this picture of your dad. Do you remember this day?"

**It could be sharing a memory they have not heard.** "Did I ever tell you about the time your mom..."

**It could be inviting their memories.** "What is your favorite thing you remember about them?"

**It could be connecting your spouse to the present.** "Your dad would be so proud of how you handled that."

**It could be talking about heaven.** "I wonder what your mom is doing right now with Jesus."

**The goal is not a deep, heavy conversation.** It is simply saying: we can talk about them. Their name belongs in our house.

**Plan when and how you will start this conversation.**
cards.reflection: **Plan a conversation about your spouse with your children this week.**

activities.title: Their Deepest Fear: Addressing the Fear of Losing You Too
activities.subtitle: Helping children manage the anxiety that comes with loss
activities.whyThisMatters: Children who lose a parent often develop intense fear of losing the surviving parent. Addressing this fear directly helps them feel secure.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Children need reassurance of continuing attachment after loss threatens their sense of security.

cards.title: The Fear Underneath Everything
cards.text:
**Your children learned something terrible when their parent died: parents can die.** People you love can disappear and never come back.

**This knowledge changes everything.** Before, death was abstract, something that happened to other people, to old people, to people in stories. Now it is real. It happened in their house, to their parent.

**And if it can happen to one parent, it can happen to the other.**

**This is often your children's deepest fear, whether they express it or not.** What if you die too? What would happen to them? Who would take care of them? Would they be alone?

**You may see this fear in clinginess.** In anxiety when you leave. In repeated questions about your health. In nightmares. In resistance to you going anywhere without them.

**This fear is logical.** It is evidence that your children understand the stakes. It needs to be addressed directly, not dismissed.

**Scripture speaks to fear.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3|When I am afraid, I put my trust in you). Your children can learn to bring their fear to God. But first, they need to be able to bring it to you.

cards.title: Answering the Unanswerable
cards.text:
Your children may ask: "Are you going to die too?"

**You cannot promise you will not.** That would be a lie. Every person dies.

**But you can offer reassurance that is honest.**

**"I plan to be here for a very long time.** I am taking care of my health. I am being careful. I am doing everything I can to be here to watch you grow up."

**"But even if something happened to me, you would be okay.** Here is who would take care of you." Name specific people. Children need a backup plan they can picture.

**"And even though we cannot know the future, we know God is watching over us.** He promises to be a 'father to the fatherless' (Psalm 68:5). Whatever happens, you will not be alone."

**Do not make promises you cannot keep.** But do make the promises you can: that you are present now, that you are taking care of yourself, that there is a plan if the worst happens, and that God will never abandon them.

cards.title: Creating Security
cards.text:
**Beyond words, you can create security through actions.**

**Maintain routines.** Predictability is safety for anxious children. Keep bedtimes, mealtimes, and rituals as consistent as possible.

**Be present when you say you will be.** If you say you will pick them up at 3:00, be there at 3:00. Every kept promise builds trust that you are reliable.

**Let them know your schedule.** Children feel more secure when they know where you are. "I will be at work until 5:00, then I will pick you up." Simple information reduces anxiety.

**Physical affection.** Hugs, cuddles, physical presence communicate safety in ways words cannot.

**Pray with them.** "God, please watch over our family. Help us trust You with our fears. Thank You that You promise to never leave us or forsake us." Teaching them to bring fear to God gives them a resource beyond you.

"The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" (Psalm 27:1|God, please watch over our family. Help us trust You with our fears. Thank You that You promise to never leave us or forsake us.). Help your children learn to say this, not as denial of fear, but as the answer to it.

cards.title: Your Children's Fears
cards.text: What signs of fear or anxiety have you noticed in your children since your spouse died?

cards.title: What Security Looks Like
cards.text:
**Think about how you can create security for your children.**

What routines or predictability can you maintain or establish?

What promises can you make and keep consistently?

How can you communicate your schedule and whereabouts in ways that reduce their anxiety?

Who are the backup caregivers your children should know about?

How can you incorporate prayer into addressing their fears?

What Scripture might help them? Psalm 23, Psalm 91, or Isaiah 41:10|Fear not, for I am with you ("Fear not, for I am with you") are often comforting for children.
cards.reflection: What practical steps can you take to create security for your anxious children?

cards.title: Addressing the Fear
cards.text:
**Plan to address your children's fear of losing you directly.**

**Choose a calm moment, not in response to a crisis.** Maybe at bedtime, when conversations often flow more easily.

**Acknowledge the fear.** "I know you might be scared that something could happen to me too. That makes sense after what happened to your dad/mom."

**Offer honest reassurance.** "I am taking care of myself. I plan to be here for a very long time."

**Provide a backup plan if appropriate.** "And if anything ever did happen, you would never be alone. [Name] would take care of you."

**Point to God.** "But most of all, I want you to know that God promises to watch over you. He says, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you' (Hebrews 13:5|Provide a backup plan if appropriate.**). No matter what happens, you are never alone."

**Invite ongoing conversation.** "Whenever you feel scared about this, you can tell me. We can talk about it and pray about it together."

**Write what you will say.**
cards.reflection: **Plan how you will address your children's fear of losing you.**

activities.title: Your Needs Matter Too: Caring for Yourself While Parenting
activities.subtitle: Why taking care of yourself is not selfish
activities.whyThisMatters: You cannot pour from an empty cup. Taking care of yourself is not selfish; it is necessary for taking care of your children.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Caregivers must care for themselves to provide sustained care for others.

cards.title: You Cannot Pour From an Empty Cup
cards.text:
**You have been told to be strong for your children.** To put their needs first. To make sure they are okay.

**But here is the truth: you cannot give what you do not have.**

**If you are depleted, exhausted, running on empty, you have nothing left for your children.** Your patience is shorter. Your presence is thinner. Your ability to be what they need is compromised.

**Taking care of yourself is not selfish.** It is necessary.

**Even Jesus withdrew to rest.** "He said to them, 'Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest'" (Mark 6:31|He said to them, 'Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest'). If Jesus needed rest, so do you.

**Your children need you for the long haul, not just today.** If you burn out, crash, break down, who will be there for them? Taking care of yourself is taking care of them.

**This is not permission to neglect your children.** It is permission to not neglect yourself. Both matter. Both need attention. The challenge is finding the balance.

cards.title: What You Need
cards.text:
What do you actually need right now? Not what your children need. What do you need?

**Rest.** Grief is exhausting. Your body needs sleep even when it will not come easily.

**Space to grieve.** You need moments when you can feel your own grief without managing your children's. This might mean a trusted friend who watches the kids so you can fall apart in private.

**Adult connection.** You need people who can support you, not just people you are supporting. Other adults who listen, who understand, who can carry some of the weight with you.

**Moments of respite.** Small things that fill you back up. A walk alone. A cup of coffee in silence. A phone call with a friend. These are not luxuries. They are necessities.

**Spiritual nourishment.** Time with God that is not just crisis prayers but actual communion. "Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28|Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest). He means you.

**You cannot survive on nothing.** Identify what you need and start figuring out how to get it.

cards.title: Asking for Help
cards.text:
**Linda did not want to ask for help.** She felt she should be able to handle her own children. Asking felt like admitting failure.

**Then she collapsed from exhaustion and ended up in the hospital for a night.** Her mother came to watch the kids. And Linda realized: she was going to need help whether she asked for it or not. Better to ask.

**You were not meant to do this alone.** Parenting was designed for two. Now you are one, and the load that was meant for two is on your shoulders.

**Scripture commands community, not isolation.** "Carry each other's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2|Carry each other's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ). Let people carry some of yours.

**Help might look like meals, childcare, someone to run errands, someone to listen, someone to sit with you in the hard moments.** It might look like a grief counselor, a support group, a church community that rallies around you.

**Asking for help is not weakness.** It is wisdom. It is also obedience to a God who designed us for interdependence.

Who can you ask?

cards.title: Your Needs
cards.text: What do you need right now that you are not getting? Be honest.

cards.title: Resources and Supports
cards.text:
**Take inventory of what resources and supports you have and what you still need.**

Who in your life can provide practical help? Childcare, meals, errands?

Who can provide emotional support? Someone to listen, to sit with you, to carry some of the weight?

Do you have time for yourself, even small amounts? If not, how could you create some?

Are you connected to a grief support group or counselor? Should you be?

Is your church community supporting you? Have you let them know what you need?

What is one need you could address this week by asking for help?
cards.reflection: What resources do you have? What do you still need? Who can you ask?

cards.title: One Act of Self-Care
cards.text:
**Commit to one act of self-care this week.**

**This does not have to be big.** It has to be real.

**Ask someone to watch the kids for an hour so you can take a walk alone.**

**Go to bed early one night instead of staying up to finish everything.**

**Call a friend who fills you up rather than depletes you.**

**Take fifteen minutes to sit in silence with God, not asking for anything, just being present.**

**Write in a journal.** Let some of what is inside come out.

**See a counselor or attend a grief group.**

**You matter.** Your needs matter. "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Matthew 22:39|Love your neighbor as yourself) assumes that you love yourself too. Not selfishly. But truly. Taking care of the person God made you to be.

What will you do this week?
cards.reflection: What one act of self-care will you commit to this week?

activities.title: New Family Rhythms: Rebuilding Routines Without Them
activities.subtitle: Creating stability in a changed family
activities.whyThisMatters: Your family's routines and rhythms have been disrupted. Creating new ones helps everyone find stability while honoring what was lost.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Families function through patterns and routines that need to be consciously rebuilt after major disruption.

cards.title: Everything Has Changed
cards.text:
**Your family used to have rhythms.** Who made breakfast. Who drove to school. Who helped with homework. Who said goodnight prayers. Who did what on Saturday mornings.

**Those rhythms were built around four people, or three, or however many you were.** Now one is missing, and everything that was built around their presence has to be rebuilt.

**This is disorienting for everyone.** Children thrive on predictability. When the routines disappear, anxiety rises. Who is in charge now? How does this work? What can I count on?

**Rebecca's husband used to make pancakes every Saturday.** After he died, Saturday mornings felt unbearable. The absence was deafening. Eventually, she started a new tradition: waffles and a trip to the park. Different. But something. A new rhythm to hold onto.

**You do not have to replace everything they did.** You do not have to pretend nothing has changed. But you do need to build new structures that give your family something to count on.

**Ecclesiastes says there is "a time to tear down and a time to build" (Ecclesiastes 3:3|a time to tear down and a time to build).** Some of your old rhythms have been torn down. Now it is time to build new ones.

cards.title: What Routines to Keep
cards.text:
**Some routines can continue even though your spouse is gone.** These provide continuity and comfort.

**Routines you did together that can still happen.** Maybe you always had pizza on Fridays. Maybe bedtime prayers happened a certain way. What can continue?

**Routines that did not depend on your spouse.** Things you already did that can stay the same.

**Rituals that honor them.** Maybe you can keep doing something they loved, in their memory. "This is what Dad/Mom always wanted to do on Sunday afternoons."

**Keeping some things the same tells your children: not everything is lost.** Some things remain. There is still something to hold onto.

**"Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever" (Hebrews 13:8|This is what Dad/Mom always wanted to do on Sunday afternoons.).** In a world where everything has changed, point your children to what does not change: God's presence, God's love, God's faithfulness.

cards.title: What Needs to Change
cards.text:
**Some routines cannot continue.** They depended on your spouse, and your spouse is not here.

**The things they always did that now fall to you.** Someone has to take over these tasks, whether you, the children, or outside help.

**The things no one can do.** Maybe your spouse had skills or time that simply cannot be replaced. You may need to let some things go or find new solutions.

**The things that are too painful.** Some routines may be so tied to your spouse that continuing them hurts more than helps. It is okay to let these go and build something new.

**Change is hard, especially for grieving children.** Involve them where possible. "Dad used to read to you at bedtime. I know it is not the same, but I would like to do it now. How does that sound?" Or: "Mom always made Sunday dinner. We cannot do it the same way, but we can still have Sunday dinner together. What should we make?"

**This is not erasing your spouse.** It is adapting to their absence. There is a difference.

cards.title: Your Family's Rhythms
cards.text: What routines in your family have been most disrupted by your spouse's death?

cards.title: Rebuilding Routines
cards.text:
**Think through your family's routines and what needs attention.**

What routines can continue as they were? What provides continuity?

What routines need to change? What depended on your spouse that now needs a new approach?

Are there routines that should be let go? Things too painful or impossible to continue?

What new routines might help? What would give your family stability and something to count on?

Are there ways to incorporate faith into your new rhythms? Prayer at meals, bedtime, or other moments?

**You do not have to figure this all out at once.** But beginning to think about it helps you move toward stability.
cards.reflection: What routines need to continue, change, or be created in your family?

cards.title: One New Rhythm
cards.text:
**Choose one new rhythm to establish with your family.**

**It could be a new mealtime routine.** Who sits where, who helps with what, what you do together.

**It could be a new bedtime routine.** How you say goodnight, whether you pray together, how you end the day.

**It could be a weekend tradition.** Something to look forward to, something that is yours as a family now.

**It could be a way of remembering your spouse.** A regular time to look at photos, tell stories, or visit a meaningful place.

**Start small.** One routine that you can commit to. Build from there.

**"Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain" (Psalm 127:1|Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain).** Invite God into your rebuilding. Ask Him to help you create a home that honors your spouse and serves your children.

What new rhythm will you start?
cards.reflection: What one new rhythm will you establish with your family?

activities.title: When You Are Not Okay: Parenting Through Your Hard Days
activities.subtitle: What to do when grief makes parenting nearly impossible
activities.whyThisMatters: Some days you will barely be able to function. Knowing what to do on those days helps you get through without harming yourself or your children.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Having plans for difficult days helps navigate them without additional damage.

cards.title: The Days When You Cannot
cards.text:
**There will be days when you cannot.**

**Days when the grief is so heavy you can barely get out of bed.** Days when the tears will not stop. Days when functioning at the most basic level takes everything you have.

**And your children will still be there.** Still needing meals, still needing supervision, still needing you.

**These days are not failures.** They are part of grief. The Psalmist wrote, "I am worn out from my groaning. All night long I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears" (Psalm 6:6|I am worn out from my groaning. All night long I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears). Some days are like that.

**But you need a plan for these days.** A way to get through them that keeps your children safe and cared for without requiring more than you have to give.

**The goal on these days is not good parenting.** It is survival. Getting through. Making sure everyone is safe until the wave passes and you can function again.

cards.title: Having a Plan
cards.text:
**When the hard days hit, you need a plan already in place.**

Who can you call? Have a short list of people who can come over on short notice. A family member, a friend, a neighbor. Someone who can take over for a few hours when you cannot.

What can your children do independently? Depending on their ages, they may be able to watch a movie, play in their rooms, or occupy themselves while you rest nearby. Know what they are capable of.

What is the minimum requirement? On the worst days, aim for safe and fed. If everyone is safe and fed, you have succeeded. Everything else can wait.

What can wait until tomorrow? Laundry, cleaning, homework help. On a crisis day, these can wait.

**Paul wrote, "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9|My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness).** On your worst days, you are utterly dependent on grace. Let that be okay.

cards.title: What to Tell Your Children
cards.text:
**On hard days, your children will notice.** You can acknowledge it without overwhelming them.

**"I am having a really sad day today because I miss your dad/mom.** Sometimes the sadness is just very big. I need to rest a little extra today."

**"This is a hard day for me.** I am going to be okay, but I need you to help by being extra good today."

**"I am feeling very tired from being sad.** We are going to have a quiet day. Is there a movie you would like to watch?"

**You do not have to hide your grief completely.** But you also do not want to frighten them or make them responsible for fixing you.

**The message you want to send: I am sad.** This is normal. I am still here for you. This will pass.

**And if you can, pray with them.** "God, today is really hard. Please help us get through it. Thank You for being with us." Let them see you bringing pain to God. That is a lesson worth teaching.

cards.title: Your Hard Days
cards.text: What has helped you get through the hardest parenting days since your spouse died?

cards.title: Your Crisis Plan
cards.text:
**Create a plan for the days when you cannot.**

Who can you call for backup? List two or three people who could come help on short notice.

What can your children do independently? Know their capabilities so you can give them something to do.

What is your minimum requirement? Define what good enough looks like on a crisis day.

What can wait? Give yourself permission to let non-essentials go.

What words will you use with your children? Have something ready so you do not have to think in the moment.

What Scripture or prayer can you hold onto? Something short that you can remember when thinking is hard. "God is our refuge and strength" (Psalm 46:1|God is our refuge and strength).
cards.reflection: **Create your crisis plan for the hardest days.**

cards.title: Prepare Your Backup
cards.text:
**Reach out to one or two people and ask if they can be your backup.**

**Explain that you are having some very hard days and you need to know someone is available if you need help with the kids.**

**This is not asking them to commit to every crisis.** It is asking if you can call when needed.

**Most people want to help but do not know how.** This gives them a specific, concrete way to support you.

**"Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor: If either of them falls down, one can help the other up" (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10|Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor: If either of them falls down, one can help the other up).** You are going to fall down sometimes. Have someone ready to help you up.

Who will you ask?
cards.reflection: Who will you ask to be your backup for hard days?

activities.title: The Hard Days Coming: Navigating Birthdays, Holidays, and Anniversaries
activities.subtitle: Preparing your family for emotionally charged occasions
activities.whyThisMatters: Special occasions are particularly difficult after losing a parent. Preparing for them helps your family navigate these days together.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Preparing for predictable difficult moments reduces their impact and improves coping.

cards.title: The Calendar Minefields
cards.text:
**Certain days are going to be hard.** You know they are coming.

**Your spouse's birthday.** The anniversary of their death. Your wedding anniversary. Your children's birthdays without their parent there. Mother's Day or Father's Day. Christmas, Thanksgiving, whatever holidays you celebrated.

**These days carry extra weight.** The absence is louder on days that are supposed to be about togetherness and celebration.

**For your children, these days are particularly complicated.** They may want to celebrate but feel guilty. They may dread the day but not know how to say so. They may not understand why everyone is sad on what is supposed to be a happy day.

**You cannot make these days easy.** But you can prepare for them. You can have a plan. You can talk about them in advance so your family is not blindsided.

**"There is a time for everything.**.. a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance" (Ecclesiastes 3:1|There is a time for everything.**.. a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance, 4). These special days will hold both mourning and, eventually, something like celebration. Both can coexist.

cards.title: Preparing Your Children
cards.text:
**Before a hard day arrives, talk to your children about it.**

**"Your mom's birthday is coming up next week.** I know it might be a sad day because we cannot celebrate with her. How are you feeling about it?"

**"Christmas is coming.** It is going to be different without Dad. I want us to talk about what we want to do."

**Give them permission to feel however they feel.** They might be sad. They might be okay. They might be both.

**Ask what they want.** Do they want to do something special to remember their parent? Do they want to keep things as normal as possible? Do they want to skip traditions or keep them?

**There is no right answer.** What matters is that they feel heard and that the day does not ambush them.

**"Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed" (Proverbs 15:22|Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed).** Your children are your advisers here. Include them in the planning.

cards.title: Creating New Traditions
cards.text:
**Some families find it helpful to create new traditions that honor the deceased parent while acknowledging the changed family.**

**Visit the cemetery together on their birthday or the anniversary.**

**Light a candle for them at holiday meals.** "This candle is to remember Dad, who we wish was here with us."

**Tell stories about them.** "Let us each share a favorite memory of Mom."

**Do something they loved.** If they loved the beach, go to the beach on their birthday. If they loved a certain meal, make that meal together.

**Contribute to something they cared about.** Make a donation or do a service project in their honor.

**These traditions acknowledge the loss while giving your family something to do with their grief.** They turn painful days into days of remembrance and connection.

**The biblical feasts were days of remembering what God had done.** You can create your own days of remembering what your spouse meant to your family.

cards.title: Your Difficult Days
cards.text: What specific dates or occasions are you most dreading with your children?

cards.title: Planning for Special Days
cards.text:
**Think through how you want to approach the difficult days ahead.**

What days are coming that will be particularly hard?

How will you prepare your children? What conversations need to happen?

What traditions do you want to keep? What should change?

Are there new traditions that might help your family honor your spouse while navigating grief?

What support do you need on these days? Who should be with you?

How can you incorporate faith into these days? Prayer, church attendance, reading Scripture about hope and resurrection?
cards.reflection: How will you approach the difficult days ahead with your children?

cards.title: Plan for the Next One
cards.text:
**Look at your calendar and identify the next difficult day coming.**

Make a plan:

When will you talk to your children about it?

What will you do that day? Keep it normal, do something special, a combination?

Will you honor your spouse in some way? How?

Who will be with you for support?

What will you tell your children if they are struggling?

What Scripture or prayer will you lean on? Consider: "The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit" (Psalm 34:18|The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit).

**Having a plan does not make the day easy.** But it makes it navigable.
cards.reflection: **Plan for the next difficult day on your calendar.**

activities.title: You Cannot Do This Alone: Getting Help for You and Your Children
activities.subtitle: Recognizing when professional support is needed
activities.whyThisMatters: Sometimes grief requires professional help. Recognizing when you or your children need more support is an act of wisdom, not weakness.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Grief can sometimes require professional intervention to prevent complicated grief or other mental health issues.

cards.title: When Grief Needs More Help
cards.text:
**Grief is normal.** Professional help is not always needed.

**But sometimes it is.**

**For you, warning signs include: inability to function at basic levels for extended periods, thoughts of harming yourself, complete inability to care for your children, use of substances to cope, grief that intensifies rather than shifts over many months.**

**For your children, warning signs include: regression that persists or worsens over time, extreme behavior changes, talk of wanting to die or join their parent, complete refusal to acknowledge the death, inability to function at school or with friends, persistent physical symptoms without medical cause.**

**These signs do not mean you or your children are broken.** They mean the grief is particularly heavy and could benefit from professional support.

**Seeking help is not failure.** It is wisdom. "Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety" (Proverbs 11:14|Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety).

cards.title: Types of Help Available
cards.text:
**Different types of support serve different needs.**

**Individual counseling: A therapist who specializes in grief can help you process your loss.** For children, a child psychologist or play therapist can help them express and work through grief.

**Grief support groups: Being with others who have experienced similar loss can be powerful.** Groups exist for widowed people and for children who have lost parents. Your children might benefit from knowing they are not alone.

**Church support: Many churches have grief ministries, Stephen Ministers, or pastoral care specifically for those who are mourning.** Do not overlook this resource.

**Online resources: Books, websites, and online communities can provide support and education about grief.**

**School counselors: If your children are struggling at school, the school counselor may be able to help or refer to additional resources.**

**God provides help through many channels.** "Every good and perfect gift is from above" (James 1:17|Every good and perfect gift is from above). Professional help, community support, church care, these are all gifts.

cards.title: Getting Help for Your Children
cards.text:
**Marcus noticed his daughter was not bouncing back.** Six months after her mother's death, she was still refusing to go to school, having nightmares every night, and barely eating. He finally took her to a child psychologist who specialized in grief. Within a few months, she was doing better. He wished he had not waited so long.

**Your children may need more help than you can provide.**

**A grief counselor can give them a safe space to express feelings they might hide from you, wanting to protect you.**

**A support group with other kids who have lost parents can help them feel less alone.**

**Sometimes children will talk to a professional in ways they will not talk to a grieving parent.** This is not rejection of you. It is developmental normalcy.

**Getting your children help is good parenting, not an admission of failure.** You cannot be everything for them right now. No one person can be. Accept that and find them the additional support they need.

cards.title: Assessing Need
cards.text: Are there signs that you or your children might benefit from professional support?

cards.title: Support Inventory
cards.text:
**Take inventory of the support you and your children currently have and what might be missing.**

For yourself: Do you have someone to talk to about your grief? Are there signs you need professional help? What resources have you not explored that might help?

For your children: How are they coping? Any warning signs? Do they have anyone outside the family they can talk to? Would they benefit from a grief group or counseling? Has their school been informed and supportive?

For your family: Are you connected to a faith community that is supporting you? Do you have practical help with the demands of daily life? What is missing?
cards.reflection: What support do you and your children have? What is missing?

cards.title: One Step Toward Help
cards.text:
**Take one step toward getting more support this week.**

**Research grief counselors in your area, for yourself or your children.**

**Find a grief support group and attend, or find one for your children.**

**Talk to your pastor about grief support available through your church.**

**Contact your children's school to ensure teachers know what has happened and are watching for struggles.**

**Call a friend and ask for specific help you need.**

**Schedule an appointment with your doctor if grief is affecting your physical health.**

**You do not have to do everything.** Pick one step and take it.

**"Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2|Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ).** Let others help you bear this.

What step will you take?
cards.reflection: What one step will you take toward getting more support?

activities.title: Hope for Your Family: Moving Forward Together
activities.subtitle: Believing in a future while honoring the past
activities.whyThisMatters: Your family has a future, even though it is not the one you planned. This activity helps you hold onto hope for what is ahead.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Hope for the future can coexist with grief for the past and must be cultivated intentionally.

cards.title: What You Have Done
cards.text:
**Through this journey, you have done significant work.**

**You have acknowledged the impossible task you face and given yourself permission to be imperfect at it.**

**You have learned how your children grieve at their different ages and stages.** You have found ways to talk about your spouse with them, keeping their parent's memory alive.

**You have addressed their deepest fears and considered how to care for yourself while caring for them.** You have begun building new family rhythms.

**You have made plans for the hard days and the special occasions.** You have considered when professional help is needed.

**This is hard, holy work.** It is the work of parenting through grief, and you are doing it.

**"I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me" (Philippians 4:13|I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me).** Not in your own strength. In His. You have made it this far. You will make it further.

cards.title: Your Family Has a Future
cards.text:
**The family you planned is gone.** But your family is not over.

**You and your children are still a family.** A grieving family, a changed family, a family with a gaping hole in it. But a family.

**Your children will grow up.** They will pass milestones their parent will not see. They will graduate, get jobs, maybe get married, maybe have children of their own. And you will be there.

**Your family will have more happy moments.** Laughter will return to your house. Joy will find its way back in. Not because you have forgotten or moved on, but because life contains both grief and joy, and your family will experience both.

**This future is not the one you planned.** But it is still a future. And God is in it.

**"'For I know the plans I have for you,' declares the Lord, 'plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future'" (Jeremiah 29:11|'For I know the plans I have for you,' declares the Lord, 'plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future').** He is still planning for your family. Trust that.

cards.title: What Your Children Will Remember
cards.text:
**Years from now, your children will remember this season.**

**They will not remember whether the house was clean.** They will not remember whether you made perfect dinners or kept up with laundry.

**They will remember whether you were present.** Whether you talked about their parent. Whether you let them grieve. Whether you loved them through the hardest time of their lives.

**They will remember how you handled this.** And they will learn from it. They will learn how to face loss, how to grieve with hope, how to lean on God when everything falls apart.

**This is the gift you can give them: not a pain-free childhood, which was never possible anyway.** But a model of faith in suffering. A demonstration that grief and hope can coexist. A living example of "we do not grieve as those who have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13|we do not grieve as those who have no hope).

**You are teaching them something no classroom can.** You are showing them how to survive the worst and still believe.

cards.title: Your Hope for Your Family
cards.text:
What do you hope for your family moving forward?

For your children: What do you hope they will carry from this experience? What do you hope they will know about their parent? What do you hope they will understand about grief, about faith, about love?

For yourself: What do you hope for your own journey through this? What kind of parent do you hope to be to them?

For your family together: What do you hope your family will become? How do you hope you will honor your spouse while building a future?

**Write your hopes.** They are seeds you are planting. Water them with faith.
cards.reflection: What do you hope for your family moving forward?

cards.title: A Prayer for Your Family
cards.text:
God,

**You see my family.** You see our grief. You see the weight I carry as I try to parent through the worst season of my life.

**Thank You for being "a father to the fatherless" (Psalm 68:5|a father to the fatherless).** My children have lost a parent, but they have not lost You. Be close to them. Comfort them in ways I cannot.

**Help me be present for them even when I am struggling.** Give me wisdom to know what they need. Give me strength to provide it.

**Help us honor their parent's memory.** Keep their stories alive in our home. Let my children grow up knowing they came from someone who loved them.

**I trust You with our future.** It is not the future we planned, but it is still in Your hands. "You hold me by my right hand. You guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will take me into glory" (Psalm 73:23-24|You hold me by my right hand. You guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will take me into glory). Hold us. Guide us.

**In Jesus' name, Amen.**

**Write your own prayer for your family.**
cards.reflection: **Write your prayer for your family.**

cards.title: Your Commitment to Your Children
cards.text:
**Make a commitment to your children.**

**I will be present with you, even when I am grieving.**

**I will talk about your parent so you never forget who they were.**

**I will give you permission to grieve however you need to.**

**I will take care of myself so I can take care of you.**

**I will ask for help when we need it.**

**I will trust God with our family's future, even when I cannot see it.**

**I will show you that grief and hope can live together, because that is what our faith teaches.**

**I love you.** We are going to get through this. Together.

**Write your commitment in your own words.** Consider sharing it with your children when the time is right.
cards.reflection: **Write your commitment to your children.**
